findings.quote: a surface gives a normal force and maybe friction, a rope gives tension, and a hand gives a push.
findings.problem: The free-body method tells the student to draw friction and tension and, in the next step, to draw each arrow in its true direction. Since the split, this lesson never says what friction or tension is, which way each points, or when a surface gives friction (the word 'maybe' has no condition). That teaching moved word for word to lesson-physics-friction-tension-and-inclines, and this lesson never names that lesson. So a student using the method here cannot place these two arrows, and the reuse rule is not met: no local teaching, no named lesson that teaches it.
findings.source: Checklist L25; LSG Teaching completeness (reuse needs an identified lesson); split diff 026f6fda removed the Tension and Friction teaching from this file

findings.quote: Split any arrow that is not along an axis into components, using $F\cos\theta$ and $F\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ measured from an axis.
findings.problem: The lesson teaches splitting an angled force here, in Core Concept ('Forces at an angle are added by components'), and slope axes in step 5, but no worked example in this lesson splits a force or uses slope axes. All six examples are along one axis. The two examples that did this, the incline and the angled pull, moved to lesson-physics-friction-tension-and-inclines, and nothing here names that lesson. Trap #3 also says the normal force 'is different on a slope' with no worked case or pointer. This reopens the round-2 L18 Major (angled force taught but never worked), which was closed by the angled-pull example that has now moved out. The brief's free-body item, which this part keeps, asks for an isolated-object force construction with components.
findings.source: Checklist L18; writer-rules.md lead ruling 1 (standard application of a skill in the lesson's goal); brief: 'add an explicit isolated-object force construction with components before combined force use'; reads/round-2 L18

findings.quote: A larger mass is harder to speed up or slow down.

The opening Dynamics paragraph, the components paragraph ('Suppose a force $F$ points...'), the first-law paragraph, the second-law units paragraph ('Here $\sum \vec F$ is the net force...') and the Trap #1 explanation also have four each.
